l: Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: The document presents Knowledge Graph Induction (KGI), an end-to-end zero-shot slot-filling system for automatically building high-quality knowledge graphs from document collections. Slot filling, a Knowledge Base Population task, identifies predetermined relations for an entity and finds their fillers in a corpus to populate infobox-like structures. KGI combines Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR), which retrieves supporting passages, with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), which generates the target tail entity from retrieved evidence. The document begins by positioning KGI against language-model and retrieval-based methods including RAG, KILT, Multi-task DPR, DensePhrases, and GENRE. Although RAG is a strong KILT baseline for generating fillers, its retrieval is weaker than BM25. KGI trains DPR and RAG in two phases using KILT provenance ground truth and target tail entities. DPR uses separate BERT-based query and passage encoders, positive passages, hard negatives, and batch negatives; passages are encoded and indexed with HNSW in FAISS. Rather than mining hard negatives with BM25 alone, KGI introduces Dense Negative Sampling, which draws difficult negatives from a learned dense index. RAG retrieves five passages and trains its query encoder through the retrieved passages’ effect on generating the correct entity. Experiments evaluate zero-shot slot filling on T-REx and zsRE using accuracy, F1, provenance quality, and combined KILT metrics. KGI1 surpasses earlier systems, especially when correct provenance is required. DPRDNS+RAG achieves the best reported results on both datasets, and KGI ranks first on the KILT leaderboard. Reported KILT-F1 improvements over previously submitted systems are 38.24% on T-REx and 21.25% on zsRE. The analysis shows that KGI1 performs best when given gold passages but worst with random passages, indicating strong use of explicit retrieved knowledge and less dependence on implicit knowledge. Explicit evidence is particularly useful for relations such as performer, author, and place of birth, while taxonomy and language relations are often handled by the language model. Finally, the work adapts a pretrained DPR to a new TACRED slot-filling variant by indexing a new corpus. KGI1 exceeds ranking baselines in zero-shot adaptation and improves further with rapid few-shot fine-tuning. The authors release pretrained models, source code, and the zero/few-shot TACRED benchmark.

l: knowledge graphs, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Knowledge graphs are the target of automatic induction from collections of documents, a task described as challenging in AI.

l: Slot filling, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Slot filling is a Knowledge Base Population sub-task that fills a missing value in an entity query of the form [ENTITY, SLOT, ?]. It recognizes a predetermined set of relations for an entity, explores a corpus for occurrences of that entity, gathers slot fillers from surrounding context, and populates infobox-like structures, sometimes with evidence text explaining predictions. Common pipelines use relation extraction; recent end-to-end approaches use retrieval-based language models. The task is developed through retrieval of relevant passages for head-and-relation queries and prediction of the ground-truth tail entity, including dense passage retrieval with hard negatives and robust training. Zero-shot work uses pre-trained transformers and language models as knowledge sources, while retrieval-augmented systems can provide textual provenance. Evaluation measures answer accuracy, token-level F1 with partial credit for overlapping tokens, and whether evidence supports generated slot fillers, including KILT benchmarks and a zero/few-shot TACRED variant.

l: retrieval-based language models, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: is_a language models [used in recent end-to-end slot filling systems] Retrieval-based language models are used by recent work to solve slot filling in an end-to-end fashion.

l: DPR, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) is a retrieval method used to retrieve evidence passages for slot filling and before answer generation. It is trained for slot filling without retrieval-specific pre-training; a baseline passage encoder is trained on Natural Questions. DPR trains query and passage encoders, and its zero-shot slot-filling approach extends dense retrieval with hard negatives, including negatives mined from a learned dense index. Models are compared using Natural Questions, BM25 hard negatives, and dense-index hard negatives; further RAG training improves retrieval. KGI uses DPR, trains encoders with KILT provenance ground truth, and during domain adaptation indexes a new corpus with pretrained DPR. Training uses two epochs and takes 24 hours on one NVIDIA V100 GPU. Finally, DPR indexes the TACRED corpus for analysis.

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Retrieval augmented generation models are trained with robust procedures in the proposed approach. The resulting model improves passage retrieval and slot value generation. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is part of KGI’s end-to-end slot filling system. The unit states that limited retrieval performance affects the generation of the slot filler.

l: T-REx, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: T-REx is a slot-filling dataset and one of two zero-shot slot-filling tasks standardized by KILT. Its train split has 2.284 million instances, making it larger than zsRE, though experiments use only its first 500,000 training instances and the datasets have similar numbers of distinct relations. It is used to evaluate slot-filling accuracy, retrieval, and the effects of explicit knowledge across relations and entity-frequency groups. DPRDNS+RAG achieves the listed best retrieval results, 74.34 R-Prec and 82.89 R@5. KGI1 substantially outperforms BARTLARGE, while knowledge gains show no consistent entity-frequency pattern; KGI ranks top-1 with a 38.24-point KILT-F1 improvement.

l: zsRE, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: zsRE is a zero-shot slot-filling dataset and one of two such tasks standardized by KILT, with 148K train-split instances. It serves evaluation of KGI, which reports a 21.25-point KILT-F1 improvement over previously submitted systems. For retrieval, DPRDNS+RAG achieves table-best 98.60 R-Prec and 99.70 R@5. DPR training takes about two hours on one NVIDIA V100; RAG training on 147,000 instances takes about 15 hours on one NVIDIA P100. KGI finishes top-1 on the KILT leaderboard.

l: KILT leaderboard, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: has_ranking_position top-1 The model ranks at the top-1 position on the KILT leaderboard.

l: TACRED, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: TACRED is a dataset and benchmark adapted from a supervised relation-extraction dataset into a new zero-shot and few-shot slot-filling variant for evaluating domain adaptation. It has the TACRED relation schema with 41 relation types and 2,673 test instances. Its corpus, relation labels, entity candidates, and annotated triples support evaluation of transfer to a different textual style and relation schema. No-relation instances are excluded from the ground-truth KG but retained in the corpus. Its supervised relation-extraction model was evaluated competitively against TAC-KBP 2015.

l: domain adaptation, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Domain adaptation in KGI replaces the original Wikipedia index by indexing a new corpus with pretrained DPR. KGI1 is transferred from Wikipedia-style data and Wikidata relations to TACRED passages and relations, enabling zero-shot slot filling for a new schema and evaluation in zero- and few-shot settings. Providing a few examples per relation quickly improves performance. The work concludes by identifying combined zero-/few-shot and human-in-the-loop strategies as future directions.

l: Knowledge Base Population, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Knowledge Base Population, abbreviated KBP, is the area in which slot filling is described as a sub-task.

l: entity, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: An entity is located in occurrences throughout a corpus, and information about its slot fillers is gathered from the context in which it appears.

l: relations, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Relations are a predetermined set that a slot filling system recognizes for a given entity.

l: corpus, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: contains documents The corpus contains documents in which occurrences of an input entity can be explored to gather information about its slot fillers.

l: slot fillers, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: The slot filler is evaluated with accuracy and token-level F1, where partial token overlap receives partial credit. KILT-Accuracy and KILT-F1 evaluate the slot filler only when the system also supplies the correct provenance.

l: slot filling system, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: A slot filling system processes and indexes a document corpus, then is prompted with an entity and relations.

l: KGI, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: KGI (Knowledge Graph Induction) is a novel slot filling system and approach for zero-shot slot filling, based on Retrieval Augmented Generation and combining Dense Passage Retrieval with RAG. It uses BERTBASE query and passage encoders and a BARTLARGE generator, with 620 million parameters, to provide generated answers and provenance. KGI unfolds through two training phases: it first trains DPR using KILT provenance ground truth, improving retrieval with hard negatives from the dense index; it then trains sequence-to-sequence generation and further trains the shared query encoder using the target tail entity. Trained on KILT data, it was evaluated on T-REx and zsRE, ranked top-1 on the KILT leaderboard, and improved KILT-F1 by 38.24 and 21.25 percentage points, respectively. It also proposed and released a TACRED-based zero/few-shot slot filling benchmark, achieved better zero-shot results than baselines there, and supports rapid few-shot fine-tuning and domain adaptation.

l: KILT, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: KILT is a benchmark and suite of benchmarks for zero-shot slot filling that standardizes zsRE and T-REx. It supplies an evaluation framework, slot-filling data, provenance annotations for positive passages, and a knowledge source of approximately 32 million passages for vector generation. KILT introduces baseline approaches, with RAG performing best among them for producing slot fillers. Its provenance ground truth trains DPR in Knowledge Graph Induction, while KILT-trained DPR supports retrieval evaluation and dense hard-negative mining. The evaluation culminates in KILT-Accuracy and KILT-F1, which credit slot fillers only when correct provenance is provided, enabling comparisons including KGI, DensePhrases, GENRE, Multi-DPR, RAG, and BARTLARGE.

l: relation extraction, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: is_a component of knowledge base population systems Relation extraction is described as the weakest component in many pipelines for extracting relations between entities from text. The unit notes that rule-based, supervised, and distantly supervised approaches require substantial human effort.

l: hard negative mining, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Hard negative mining is a DPR training method in KGI for improving the context encoder in end-to-end slot filling. It forms a query from the head entity and relation, retrieves BM25-ranked passages with Anserini, excludes ground-truth or answer-containing passages, and selects the highest remaining result.

l: Wikipedia, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Wikipedia serves as a source corpus and index for KILT, RAG-KKS, KGI1, and TACRED-related experiments. Its entity pages concentrate many relations, making page-title generation useful for retrieval; its index can also be replaced with one built from TACRED passages.

l: RAG, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: RAG is a model for slot filling. It first uses DPR to retrieve five relevant evidence passages, concatenates each passage with the query, and uses a BART-initialized sequence-to-sequence generator to predict the tail entity or answer. It marginalizes weighted next-token distributions across passages and trains the query encoder through their contribution to the correct output. In the KILT baseline, the Natural Questions-trained passage encoder remains fixed while the query encoder and generation component are fine-tuned. RAG produces the best slot fillers among tested baselines, though its retrieval is worse than BM25. Training on 500k T-REx instances takes two days on one NVIDIA P100 GPU.

l: BARTLARGE, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: BARTLARGE is a sequence-to-sequence generation component and implicit-knowledge baseline for KILT slot filling. It takes retrieved passages with a query, predicts tokens, and combines passage token distributions weighted by retrieval scores. It is the strongest implicit baseline, but scores about 40 accuracy points below KGI1 on T-REx.

l: BM25, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: BM25 is a traditional keyword search engine that locates hard negative passages for DPR training, unlike dense vector-index retrieval.

l: Multi-task DPR, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Multi-task DPR trains DPR passage and query encoders on multiple KILT tasks, retrieves its top three passages, and combines them with the query for BART to answer, yielding large retrieval-performance gains.

l: DPR, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: DPR is a work using keyword-based hard negative mining to train encoders, then generating vectors for approximately 32 million KILT knowledge source passages.

l: hard negatives, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Hard negatives are remaining top-ranked Anserini passages excluding overlaps or correct answers, paired with queries and positive passages for additional DPR training; in Dense Negative Sampling, ANN search over a learned dense vector index mines them instead of BM25.

l: query, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: A query consists of a head entity and relation, represented in the diagram in the form "head [SEP] relation." The query is encoded independently and compared by inner product with all passages in the batch.

l: positive passage, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: is_given_by KILT [ground truth provenance] A positive passage is the passage given by the KILT ground-truth provenance. It is paired with a query and a hard negative in DPR training and is the target of the negative log-likelihood loss.

l: negative passage, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: A negative passage is a passage that is not the positive passage for a given query. The hard negative and the passages associated with other queries in the batch serve as negatives during training.

l: passage, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Passages are indexed with Anserini and retrieved using BM25; after training, about 32 million KILT knowledge source passages are encoded as vectors for retrieval.

l: batch negatives, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Batch negatives are positive and hard negative passages from other queries in the same training batch, included as negatives for each query.

l: DPR training data, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: DPR training data is a set of triples containing a query, a KILT ground-truth positive passage, and a hard negative passage.

l: passage encoder, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: is_a BERT [model] The passage encoder is a BERT model that independently encodes passages. After training, it generates vectors for approximately 32 million passages in the KILT knowledge source.

l: query encoder, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: The query encoder is a BERT model that independently encodes queries, comparing its outputs with passage representations through inner products. It is trained with the passage encoder for slot filling, then injected into RAG for Natural Questions, where retrieval-driven training updates it without disrupting generation.

l: approximate nearest neighbors, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Approximate nearest neighbors are used to index the passage vectors for retrieval. The unit identifies HNSW as the approximate nearest-neighbor data structure used through the FAISS library.

l: HNSW index, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: is_a approximate nearest neighbors [data structure] The HNSW index is an approximate nearest-neighbor data structure built with the open-source FAISS library. It indexes the passage vectors, which are reduced to 8-bit scalar quantization to lower memory usage.

l: passage vectors, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Passage vectors are generated from approximately 32 million KILT passages using a trained DPR encoder, then indexed with HNSW, FAISS, and 8-bit scalar quantization.

l: RAG for Slot Filling, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: RAG for Slot Filling predicts a ground truth tail entity from a head-and-relation query. It retrieves passages with an ANN index and uses a generator whose weighted predictions are combined before beam search selects the tail entity.

l: FAISS index, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: FAISS index retrieves top five passages by query-passage inner product and mines hard negatives for Dense Negative Sampling, requiring 256GB memory without scalar quantization.

l: Dense Negative Sampling, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: uses hard negatives [found by ANN search over the learned dense vector index] Dense Negative Sampling mines hard negatives by searching a learned dense vector index with ANN rather than locating negatives with BM25. DNS initially lowers T-REx retrieval performance relative to DPRBM25, but DNS followed by RAG training produces the best reported performance on T-REx and zsRE.

l: DPRDNS, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: has_retrieval_performance 42.62 R-Prec and 55.09 R@5 on T-REx [immediately after DNS training] DPRDNS is the DPR model immediately after Dense Negative Sampling training. It reaches 42.62 R-Prec and 55.09 R@5 on T-REx and 97.53 R-Prec and 99.30 R@5 on zsRE before additional RAG training.

l: RAG training, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: trains query encoder [through its impact in generation] RAG training provides weak supervision based on a passage’s impact on producing the correct answer rather than on ground truth provenance. It substantially improves retrieval after DPR or DNS training, especially when applied to DPRDNS.

l: DNS training, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: trains context encoder [when negatives are drawn from the dense vector index] DNS training is performed for two additional epochs using hard negatives retrieved from the learned dense index. It is the only training applied to the context encoder when negatives are drawn from the dense vector index.

l: retrieval, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Slot filling evaluation measures retrieval with R-Precision and Recall@5 on T-REx and zsRE, comparing RAG, BM25, DPR, and KGI methods. RAG training after DPR yields large gains, and DNS plus RAG is strongest. Analysis with random, retrieved, and gold passages shows gold retrieval greatly improves accuracy, while random retrieval harms all systems.

l: slot-filling task, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: is_framed_as ranking problem [in zero-shot TACRED evaluation] Slot filling is evaluated as the task of identifying missing values for entity-relation queries. In the TACRED adaptation, it is framed as ranking candidate slot values that co-occur with the subject in the corpus.

l: ground truth provenance, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Provenance identifies the passages supporting a slot-filling answer and is evaluated against KILT ground truth. Systems other than RAG-KKS provide provenance for their top answer, and correct provenance is required for the combined KILT metrics.

l: KILT knowledge source, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: is_a 2019/08/01 Wikipedia snapshot The KILT knowledge source is a 2019/08/01 Wikipedia snapshot whose documents are segmented into passages. Passages are aligned with paragraph boundaries when possible, with short paragraphs combined and overly long paragraphs truncated.

l: KGI0, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: uses_hard_negatives_from BM25 [for DPR training] KGI0 uses DPR trained with hard negative samples from BM25. On the development sets, it achieves higher retrieval and slot-filling performance than the RAG baselines on both zsRE and T-REx.

l: KGI1, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: KGI1 is a model for slot filling that uses explicit knowledge and DPR-trained retrieval, including dynamic negative sampling, to generate restricted candidate fillers with justifying evidence. It improves slot-filling accuracy and combined KILT metrics over earlier systems, reaching the strongest reported development performance among listed KGI systems. On T-REx, it greatly outperforms BARTLARGE and performs best with gold passages, less well with retrieved passages, and worst with random passages, reflecting a tradeoff from implicit to explicit knowledge. It supports zero-shot TACRED and human-in-the-loop candidate filling, surpasses ranking baselines, and improves further with few-shot examples.

l: Wikidata, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Wikidata is the knowledge-graph source associated with the original tasks. The TACRED relations differ from those in Wikidata.

l: explicit knowledge, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Explicit knowledge improves slot filling, especially for relations not central to an entity’s meaning or predictable from surface features. Its value depends on relation rather than entity corpus frequency, and is greatest for performer and author.

l: implicit knowledge, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: is_encoded_in language model [for essential entity properties] Implicit knowledge is encoded in the language model and can support relations such as taxonomy, partonomy, and languages spoken, written, or signed. KGI1 sacrifices some implicit-knowledge performance in exchange for stronger use of explicit knowledge.

l: zero-shot learning, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Zero-shot learning is evaluated on TACRED without task-specific training examples for KGI1. KGI1 achieves a HIT@1 score of 28.51 and higher HIT@5 and HIT@10 scores than the PMI, Word2Vec, and GPT-2 baselines.

l: few-shot learning, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Few-shot learning is tested by fine-tuning KGI1 with one or four randomly selected training examples for each TACRED relation. HIT@1 improves by approximately five and ten percentage points, respectively, compared with the zero-shot result.

l: zero-shot slot filling, Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: Zero-shot slot filling is the task addressed by KGI, which is introduced as a novel approach for this setting. The paper evaluates the approach on T-REx, zsRE, and a new TACRED-based benchmark.

l: zero/few-shot slot filling benchmark (based on TACRED), Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
s: A TACRED-based zero/few-shot slot filling benchmark was proposed and released to evaluate domain adaptation; KGI achieved much better zero-shot results than baselines.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: This paper introduces multilingual keyphrase generation: using one model to predict keyphrases in the same language as an input long text across German, Spanish, Italian, French, Korean, and Chinese. It aims to reduce annotation, training, and deployment costs and alleviate low-resource scarcity through joint multilingual training. The study contributes EcommerceMKP, with 73,000 e-commerce examples in Spanish, German, Italian, and French, and AcademicMKP, with 2,693 Chinese and Korean academic papers. Its central method is the Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generator (RAMKG). It retrieves related English passages through Cross-Lingual Dense Passage Retrieval, then uses mBART to generate keyphrases from the source passage and retrieved English keyphrases. English passage-keyphrase resources supply external knowledge across e-commerce and academic topics, addressing multilingual retrieval difficulties caused by vocabulary gaps. Because bilingual data is limited, retriever-generator iterative training (RGIT) mines pseudo-parallel passage pairs to improve the retriever and, in turn, generation. The paper details dataset collection and cleaning, English retrieval resources, generation and retrieval metrics, and comparisons with statistical, graph-based, feature-based, neural, Transformer, Copy-RNN, mBART, and RAMKG variants. Results show supervised methods beating unsupervised ones; Transformer surpassing Copy-RNN; and jointly trained mBART exceeding monolingual mBART. RAMKG achieves higher average precision, recall, and F1 than the listed mBART variants on both datasets, while RGIT further improves retrieval and generation. However, external English data has no positive effect on AcademicMKP. A German EcommerceMKP case study finds that retrieved English keyphrases offer useful information despite some noise. The paper concludes that its datasets and retrieval-augmented framework outperform a broad range of baselines.

l: Keyphrase Generation, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Keyphrase Generation is a task of automatically predicting keyphrases from long text, using neural language generation to model phrase importance and semantics rather than merely extract substrings. Existing work has focused mainly on English, while this work extends investigation to multiple other languages. Methods have evolved through attention, structural and decoding mechanisms, alignment, and pre-trained language models; retrieval can improve accuracy. Evaluation uses exact-match precision, recall, and F1 over predicted and gold keyphrase sets across languages. Results show supervised methods outperform unsupervised ones, multilingual Transformer outperforms Copy-RNN, and better retrieved English keyphrases improve performance.

l: multilingual keyphrase generation, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Multilingual keyphrase generation is a new, under-explored task setting that predicts keyphrases in the source language of an input text. It covers German, Spanish, Italian, French, Korean, and Chinese, and is constrained by limited non-English text, domain-specific annotations, and datasets. The study introduces two datasets and evaluates supervised methods, joint multilingual training, and a retrieval-augmented framework across six languages and two domains. The framework retrieves English keyphrases as external knowledge and can tolerate retrieval noise; in a German case study, it produces mostly correct German keyphrases despite noisy retrieved English keyphrases. The work concludes by establishing and investigating this novel setting.

l: EcommerceMKP, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: EcommerceMKP is a multilingual e-commerce keyphrase-generation dataset spanning German, Spanish, French, and Italian, with about 73,000 product examples. It uses product titles, descriptions, and bullet descriptions as source input; target keyphrases come from purchase-producing user search queries, are chunked with AutoPhrase, ranked by frequency, and threshold-filtered. It totals 62,368 training, 3,665 development, and 7,346 test examples. Passages average 161 in length and nine keyphrases, while 56.4% of keyphrases are absent. The dataset is one of two new contributions for multilingual keyphrase generation and is used for main results, retrieval, pseudo parallel passage mining, iterative training, and a German case study. On DEV, RAMKG + RGIT raises Recall@5 from 50.1% to 72.4% and generation performance from 44.50 to 45.73.

l: AcademicMKP, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: AcademicMKP is a multilingual academic-domain keyphrase-generation dataset drawn from Microsoft Academic Graph. It contains 2,693 manually checked, high-quality computer-science papers in Chinese and Korean: titles and abstracts are source texts, and author-provided keyphrases or keywords are targets. The data comprise 1,884 training, 268 development, and 541 test examples, with passages averaging 171 in length, four keyphrases, and 31.3% absent keyphrases. It is one of two new datasets for multilingual keyphrase generation and is part of a six-language collection. It is used to evaluate multilingual approaches; external English data does not improve results, attributed to a domain gap with English papers in KP20K.

l: non-English languages, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Non-English languages have not been extensively investigated for keyphrase generation. The proposed method uses English dataset annotations to support keyphrase generation in low-resource non-English languages.

l: RAMKG, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: RAMKG is a retrieval-augmented multilingual keyphrase generation framework and method designed to mitigate data shortages in non-English languages. Given a non-English source passage, it uses Cross-Lingual Dense Passage Retrieval to retrieve top relevant English passages and their English keyphrase annotations. It combines the source passage with retrieved English keyphrases as code-mixed input and uses mBART to generate keyphrases in the source language. Rather than only infusing external knowledge into model parameters, it supplies auxiliary knowledge directly to the generation module. RAMKG uses retriever-generator iterative training through RGIT. It outperforms EN Joint Train, EN Pretrain, and a wide range of baselines; on EcommerceMKP it reports average precision, recall, and F1 of 48.59, 44.61, and 44.50, and on AcademicMKP 31.31, 30.82, and 30.49.

l: data shortage problem, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: is_used_to_alleviate resource scarcity [through joint training of multiple languages] The data shortage problem affects keyphrase generation in non-English languages. The proposed retrieval-augmented method is designed to mitigate this problem.

l: English datasets, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: English datasets provide keyphrase annotations that the retrieval-augmented model uses as external knowledge to facilitate keyphrase generation in low-resource languages. English datasets are described as large-scale resources containing useful keyphrase knowledge. Experiments show that they can provide beneficial external knowledge for multilingual keyphrase generation.

l: Cross-Lingual Dense Passage Retrieval, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Cross-Lingual Dense Passage Retrieval is a retrieval method and model in the RAMKG framework. Given a non-English, often low-resource, passage, it uses a query encoder to search indexed English passage encodings with KNN and FAISS, returning the top related English passages. Alignment training on parallel or mined pseudo-parallel passage pairs maps corresponding multilingual passages nearby. The retrieved passages’ associated English keyphrases then support generation in the current language.

l: keyphrases, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Keyphrases are single- or multi-word lexical units that summarize text and support indexing, categorizing, and mining. In keyphrase generation, they are target outputs and associated passage labels. A multilingual method retrieves related English passages, uses their English keyphrase annotations as external knowledge or hints, and generates concatenated target-language keyphrases with separator tokens.

l: Algorithm 1 Parallel Passage Mining via Iterative Training, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Algorithm 1 is an iterative training algorithm that strengthens cross-lingual passage retrieval by mining pseudo parallel passage pairs. It takes parallel data, non-parallel data, and a large-scale English corpus; trains a baseline generator; repeatedly trains a retriever and retrieval-augmented generator; creates pairs when retrieved keyphrases improve F1 beyond τ; and returns pseudo-parallel data. Passage mining finds about 20,000 pairs per iteration, while DEV labeling accuracy rises from 28.0% to 47.0%.

l: pseudo parallel passage pairs, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Pseudo parallel passage pairs are iteratively mined to improve retriever and generator; about 20,000 are found per iteration, and labeling accuracy rises across six iterations, reaching 47.0% on EcommerceMKP DEV.

l: cross-lingual passage retriever, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: searches knowledge base [for useful non-parametric knowledge] The cross-lingual passage retriever finds relevant English passages for non-English passages. Its performance is strengthened by the retriever-generator iterative training algorithm, which mines pseudo parallel passage pairs.

l: English, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: English supplies large-scale passages and text-keyphrase pairs, especially in e-commerce and academic paper domains, as an external knowledge base for multilingual keyphrase generation. Its passages and keyphrases are retrieved to hint at lower-resource-language keyphrases, support EcommerceMKP-EN and auxiliary training, and train a cross-lingual dense passage retriever. Retrieved English keyphrases can be useful but may introduce noise.

l: Spanish, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Spanish is a language included in a multilingual keyphrase generation study and one of four EcommerceMKP languages, with reported RAMKG + RGIT results.

l: German, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: German is a language used in a multilingual keyphrase-generation study. It is one of four EcommerceMKP languages, where RAMKG + RGIT achieves 48.11 precision, 43.05 recall, and 43.30 F1. In a case study, it accurately generates gold keyphrases but incorrectly adds “jimmy.”

l: Italian, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Italian is a language included in a multilingual keyphrase generation study and one of four EcommerceMKP languages, with reported RAMKG + RGIT results.

l: French, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: French is a language studied for multilingual keyphrase generation and one of four EcommerceMKP languages, with reported RAMKG + RGIT results.

l: Chinese, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Chinese is a language studied in multilingual keyphrase generation, represented in AcademicMKP with reported RAMKG + RGIT precision, recall, and F1.

l: Korean, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Korean is a language included in a multilingual keyphrase generation study and AcademicMKP, where RAMKG + RGIT achieves 28.00 F1.

l: retriever-generator iterative training, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Retriever-generator iterative training is an iterative-training method for keyphrase generation that automatically mines pseudo training parallel passage pairs from unlabeled data to address scarce parallel passage-keyphrase data. It begins with a small set of initial parallel pairs, including robust results with 1.2k pairs, trains a retriever and a retrieval-augmented generator, and uses generation feedback to retain retrieved English passages whose keyphrases improve F1 beyond a threshold. It repeats retriever training, generator training, and mining, producing over 20,000 pseudo-parallel pairs in experiments. Stronger retrieval finds more relevant English keyphrases and improves retrieval and generation, though gains diminish as annotated parallel data increases. Adding RGIT to RAMKG improves reported EcommerceMKP and AcademicMKP scores.

l: retrieval-augmented keyphrase generation, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Retrieval-augmented keyphrase generation is a method for multilingual keyphrase generation that uses relatively rich English datasets as external knowledge. It first retrieves a semantically related English passage for a non-English passage, mining parallel passages through retriever-generator iterative training. It then supplies the original passage and retrieved English keyphrases as code-mixed input to a generator, which predicts keyphrases in the original language. Retrieved keyphrases provide supplementary hints based on shared topics or concepts, while the generator can emphasize informative content and tolerate retrieval noise.

l: multilingual keyphrase generation datasets, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: The study introduces EcommerceMKP and AcademicMKP, two publicly available multilingual keyphrase generation datasets spanning six languages and two domains, addressing a training and benchmarking gap.

l: e-commerce domain, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: In the e-commerce domain, bilingual product descriptions for products sold in both English and another marketplace are treated as parallel passage pairs. The text notes that the same products and their keyphrases can share semantic similarity across marketplaces and countries. It provides the setting from which EcommerceMKP is collected. Product text and purchase-producing search queries from a popular E-commerce shopping platform are used to construct the dataset.

l: CopyRNN, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: CopyRNN is a neural supervised keyphrase generation model proposed by Meng et al. (2017). It generates vocabulary words and points to source-text words, addressing absent keyphrases. It attains high precision among supervised approaches, though Transformer greatly outperforms it in multilingual use.

l: Retrieval Augmented Text Generation, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Retrieval Augmented Text Generation is an approach for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks that combines pre-training knowledge with useful non-parametric knowledge retrieved sparsely or densely, supporting question answering, fact checking, entity linking, and keyphrase generation.

l: English keyphrase knowledge base, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: English keyphrase knowledge base forms from passage-keyphrase pairs across topics, supplying retrieved English passages and high-quality associated keyphrases for the multilingual generator.

l: EcommerceMKP-EN, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: An English keyphrase generation dataset collected under EcommerceMKP’s protocol, containing 3 million passage-keyphrase pairs; it supplies joint-training or pretraining data and is searched as external knowledge to retrieve relevant passages and keyphrases.

l: Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Code-Mixed Inputs, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Code-Mixed Inputs is the setting addressed by the RAMKG framework. The framework uses retrieved English passage-keyphrase pairs to support keyphrase generation in this setting.

l: single multilingual keyphrase generation model, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: A model generates keyphrases in any trained language, aiming to reduce annotation costs, avoid separate models, and benefit from joint multilingual training.

l: text, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: The text is provided in one of the study's supported languages. Its corresponding keyphrases are predicted in that same language.

l: mBART, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: mBART is a multilingual denoising pre-trained sequence-to-sequence language model used for multilingual keyphrase generation. It takes retrieved English keyphrases and a source passage separated by special tokens, then generates target-language keyphrases. Across monolingual, multilingual, English-joint-training, and English-pretraining evaluations, joint multilingual training generally outperforms separate monolingual training, indicating cross-language transfer of key-information locating and summarizing ability.

l: mBERT, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: mBERT is a multilingual pre-trained BERT-based dense passage retriever that encodes passages into 768-dimensional vectors; initially unaligned across languages, it is trained with bilingual positives and English negatives.

l: academic paper domain, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: In the academic paper domain, scarce parallel text leads to pseudo-parallel abstract-pair mining with Sentence Transformers, LaBSE, nearest-neighbor retrieval, and a margin threshold, supporting AcademicMKP datasets built from paper titles, abstracts, and author-provided keywords.

l: parallel passage mining, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Parallel passage mining measures retrieved English passages by keyphrase generation, then iteratively selects those improving non-English predictions to produce pseudo parallel pairs for retrieval and generation.

l: KP20K, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: KP20K is a keyphrase generation dataset of 560k computer science abstract-keyphrase pairs, used in AcademicMKP for English retrieval-augmented generation and passage mining.

l: Microsoft Academic Graph, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: is_a academic domain [web-scale academic entity graph] It is the source from which AcademicMKP papers are sampled. Because some of its automatically crawled data are noisy, samples are manually examined, incomplete abstracts are removed, and metadata and keyphrase information are corrected when needed.

l: mBART + EN Joint Train, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: is_a keyphrase generation [jointly trained model] It is jointly trained on the multilingual data and English data, using EcommerceMKP-EN for EcommerceMKP and KP20K for AcademicMKP. Its reported average F1 is 43.08 on EcommerceMKP and 28.73 on AcademicMKP.

l: mBART + EN Pretrain, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: is_a keyphrase generation [English-pretrained model] It is first pretrained on English data and then fine-tuned on the multilingual data. Its reported average F1 is 43.47 on EcommerceMKP and 28.68 on AcademicMKP.

l: Transformer, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Transformer is a neural-based supervised keyphrase generation approach that outperforms Copy-RNN by a large margin in multilingual results.

l: computer science, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: It is the academic field used for the high-quality AcademicMKP examples. KP20K also contains abstracts and keyphrases from computer science papers.

l: keyphrase extraction, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: It is represented by unsupervised statistical, unsupervised graph-based, and supervised feature-based baselines. The listed methods include KP-Miner, YAKE, TextRank, TopicalPageRank, PositionRank, MultipartiteRank, and KEA.

l: passage retrieval, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Passage retrieval for keyphrase generation is evaluated by top-k recall on development sets to assess external knowledge use. Mined pseudo-parallel passage pairs substantially improve EcommerceMKP DEV Recall@5 from 50.1% to 72.4%, while iterative training improves with more annotated parallel data.

l: study, Retrieval-Augmented Multilingual Keyphrase Generation with Retriever-Generator Iterative Training
s: Study introduces multilingual keyphrase generation, releases two datasets, and proposes iterative retriever-generator training that outperforms many baselines.

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: “Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding,” by Wenyu Huang, Mirella Lapata, Pavlos Vougiouklis, Nikos Papasarantopoulos, and Jeff Z. Pan, presents a framework for Knowledge-Intensive Generation, where a system retrieves external passages and uses them to produce natural-language answers or conversational responses. The work targets hallucination and a weakness in conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): training through retrieval marginalization can favor passages that overlap with the label answer rather than passages containing the underlying knowledge needed to produce it. This label-relevant bias can overfit retrievers and miss knowledge-relevant passages with little token overlap with an answer. The proposed RAG-based retrieve-generate model uses a Dense Passage Retriever and a BART encoder-decoder, augmented with two objectives. Retriever as Answer Classifier (RAC) trains the retriever to determine whether a retrieved passage contains knowledge expressed in the answer. Dense Knowledge Similarity (DKS) aligns question-passage representations with knowledge representations extracted from answers. Generation, answer-classification, and knowledge-similarity losses are jointly optimized with balancing weights; a multi-task variant combines the objectives. The paper situates this approach among knowledge-intensive generation and retrieval methods, including RAG, FiD, KG-FiD, KGI, RE2G, and Hindsight, while emphasizing false-negative passages, passage selection, and the need for robust retrievers. It evaluates retrieval, generation, and combined performance on MSMARCO generative QA and KILT Wizard of Wikipedia informative conversation, using MSMARCO’s 8.8M passages and about 24.5M passages from the 2019/08/01 Wikipedia dump. Metrics include recall, ROUGE-L, F1, BLEU, METEOR, R-Precision, and KILT scores. Results show improvements over RAG in retrieval and end-to-end generation. The multi-task method is strongest overall on the MSMARCO development set and on several MSMARCO metrics, while RAC obtains the highest KILT-WoW retrieval and end-to-end ROUGE-L results, and DKS achieves the highest combined scores and best KILT-WoW R-Precision. Smaller train-to-development drops indicate greater robustness. In a Gouda cheese example, RAC and DKS give knowledge-matched answers whereas RAG hallucinates goat’s milk. The authors conclude that RAC and DKS mitigate label-relevant overfitting, while noting fixed passage-encoder parameters and unavailable MSMARCO test data as limitations; future work may combine passages with structured knowledge.

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding is a work by Wenyu Huang, Pavlos Vougiouklis, Nikos Papasarantopoulos, and Jeff Z. Pan. It incorporates rich answer encoding through Dense Knowledge Similarity and Retriever as Answer Classifier, evaluates open-domain question answering and conversation, and reports improved generation and retrieval metrics on MSMARCO and Wizard of Wikipedia.

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Retrieval Augmented Generation is a modeling approach and Transformer-based retrieve-generate system for knowledge-intensive generation tasks. It retrieves external passages to support answer generation and addresses hallucination. Its backbone scores passages with a Dense Passage Retriever, selects top-n using Maximum Inner Product Search, and marginalizes token-generation probabilities to maximize a label sentence. State-of-the-art marginalized-output models may overfocus on label-relevant rather than question-relevant passages and answers; related methods add reranking, hindsight retrieval, or knowledge graphs.

l: Rich Answer Encoding, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Rich Answer Encoding represents answer knowledge for retrieval-augmented generation, shifting training from token-level to sequence- or knowledge-level matching; it supports Dense Knowledge Similarity and Retriever as Answer Classifier to incorporate answer information.

l: Knowledge-Intensive Generation, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Knowledge-Intensive Generation is a series of natural language generation tasks requiring large external knowledge sources, such as passage corpora or knowledge graphs. It matters because it combines access to question-relevant knowledge with natural-language response generation and is more challenging than fact checking and slot filling. It unfolds by retrieving question-relevant passages, then generating a response conditioned on the question and retrieved passages.

l: Generative QA, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Generative QA is a knowledge-intensive generation, or KIG, task requiring retrieval of appropriate external passages, with generation quality heavily dependent on that context. It is one of two KIG tasks used to evaluate proposed methods, on the NLGen split of MSMARCO QA with generation and retrieval metrics. Evaluation covers retrieval, end-to-end generation, robustness, and answer quality; better retrieval generally improves generation and reduces hallucination, while focus on label-relevant passages can overfit, mitigated by the training framework.

l: Dense Knowledge Similarity, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Dense Knowledge Similarity is a proposed answer-encoding method and knowledge-constrained objective for training a retriever to retrieve knowledge-relevant passages in retrieval-augmented generation. It changes the goal from generating a natural-language answer label to generating the knowledge needed to answer a question. It compares answer and passage encodings in a knowledge representation space, training a knowledge extractor to align question-passage representations with representations from gold answers through mean squared error loss, so relevant passages are closer to the answer than other passages. It uses continuous sequence-level features for conversational tasks. In experiments, it obtains 11.5 R@1 on MSMARCO and 47.02 R-Precision on KILT-WoW, the best R-Precision across models, with an 11.4% relative improvement over the baseline. It retrieves the same Wikipedia page as RAC and gives a perfect knowledge match in a sampled generation. It concludes as one of two objectives guiding retrievers toward knowledge-relevant passages.

l: Retriever as Answer Classifier, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Retriever as Answer Classifier is a proposed answer-encoding method and knowledge-constrained objective for retrieval-augmented generation. It trains a retriever to classify whether its top-n retrieved passages contain the knowledge in an answer, treating both example passages as positive. Training uses in-batch negative answers from the rest of the training set and binary cross-entropy loss. It is one of two knowledge-constrained objectives intended to guide retrieval toward knowledge-relevant passages. Evaluated against RAG and DPR, it reports 54.1 BLEU-1, 33.8 BLEU-4, and 59.0 ROUGE-L on MSMARCO; 11.2 R@1 on MSMARCO development; and 44.95 R-Precision on KILT-WoW development. In a Gouda cheese example, it retrieves the same Wikipedia page as DKS and gives a perfect knowledge match.

l: open domain question answering, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: uses_dataset MSMARCO Open domain question answering is one of the evaluation settings for the proposed approach. The experiments use MSMARCO and report generation and retrieval metrics.

l: conversation, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: uses_dataset Wizard of Wikipedia Conversation is one of the evaluation settings for the proposed approach. The experiments use Wizard of Wikipedia.

l: MSMARCO, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: MSMARCO is a well-known KIG dataset with a generative QA task, evaluated using 8.8M passages extracted from 3.6M web documents retrieved by Bing and ROUGE-L for end-to-end generation quality. Its NLGen split provides crowdworker-rewritten, well-formed answers for generative question answering. Because the challenge is retired and the full test set is unavailable, the original train split is divided into training and validation sets, with results reported on the original development split. It is used to evaluate open-domain and generative QA methods, including effectiveness and robustness. Reported best results include a 12.1% relative Recall@1 improvement and a 4.5% BLEU-4 improvement over baseline or RAG; a multi-task model reaches about 14.3% Recall@1 improvement over non-finetuned DPR and shows lower overfit than RAG.

l: Wizard of Wikipedia, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Wizard of Wikipedia is a well-known KIG dataset for informative conversation, evaluated in the KILT benchmark. It uses R-Precision for retrieval evaluation. Because its test split is unpublished, experiments generally use the public development set, while a best test result comes from the KILT leaderboard. It supports evaluation of proposed methods, which improve retrieval and generation metrics over a baseline.

l: KILT-WoW, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: KILT-WoW is a KILT evaluation dataset based on Wizard of Wikipedia, used to report retrieval and end-to-end generation results and to evaluate effectiveness, robustness, leaderboards, and case studies. On its leaderboard, the best model improves R-Precision by 8.9% and KILT-RL by 13.3% over RAG; DKS has the best R-Precision, while proposed methods improve KILT-RL and KILT-F1 and generally reduce the train-to-development gap.

l: KILT-WoW leaderboard, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: KILT-WoW leaderboard concludes that the best model surpasses the baseline by 8.9% R-Precision, 13.3% KILT-RL, and 13.2% KILT-F1.

l: Recall@1, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Recall@1 is reported for the MSMARCO robustness evaluation. The multi-task model achieves about 14.3% relative improvement, or 1.5% absolute improvement, over non-finetuned DPR on this metric.

l: R-Precision, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: is_identical_to Precision@1 [in KILT-WoW] R-Precision is used as a retrieval metric, and it is identical to Precision@1 in the KILT-WoW dataset. DKS achieves the best R-Precision across the evaluated models, with an 11.4% relative improvement over RAG in the development evaluation.

l: external knowledge sources, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: External knowledge sources support Knowledge-Intensive Generation, comprising passage corpora and knowledge graphs.

l: passage corpus, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: The passage corpus is denoted P and contains the passages from which question-relevant passages are selected. The passage corpus is the collection from which the retriever selects passages for a given question. Passage selection is performed using similarity scores and Maximum Inner Product Search.

l: large language models, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Large language models, including GPT-4, can produce plausible but factually incorrect statements when lacking external knowledge. Hallucination is the central concern. Retrieval-augmented generation, using passages or knowledge graph triples, is presented to support reasoning, improve factuality, and train retrievers to reduce hallucinations.

l: hallucination problem, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Hallucination is the generation of plausible-looking but factually incorrect statements; pretrained language models, including BART, T5, and GPT series, significantly suffer from it in knowledge-intensive generation tasks.

l: RAG, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: RAG is a retrieve-generate architecture and encoder-decoder backbone. It first retrieves question-relevant passages from external knowledge sources, then generates responses from them; at inference it uses the top-5 retrieved passages. Its retriever and generator are jointly trained under label-answer supervision, and retrieval is marginalized. RAG tends to capture label-relevant, high-token-matching passages, retrieving Passage 1 but failing to retrieve Passage 2 because of label relevance. It is compared with DPR, marginally outperforming non-finetuned DPR by 1.9% Recall@1. Used as a baseline and main comparison model, it achieves reported retrieval and generation scores on MSMARCO and KILT-WoW, but performs worse than the proposed methods, generalizes badly in robustness evaluation, and can hallucinate answers.

l: retriever, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: The retriever is an essential component of Knowledge-Intensive Generation, intended to support retrieval-augmented LLM systems by selecting passages that can verify and correct factual errors. It is jointly trained with a generator through gradients from negative log-likelihood loss, but this can bias it toward and cause overfitting to label-relevant passages. The proposed framework instead guides it, using RAC and DKS, to retrieve more knowledge-relevant passages rather than relying only on label-relevant ones. This more robust training improves generalization and yields consistent retrieval-quality improvements on MSMARCO and KILT Wizard of Wikipedia.

l: reference answer, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Tactful describes someone or something showing regard for other people’s feelings; this reference answer defines the term while explaining that retrieved knowledge should support generating the answer.

l: knowledge-relevant passages, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Knowledge-relevant passages are a subset of question-relevant passages containing the information needed to generate a label answer. Introduced as passages that may express answer knowledge despite little wording overlap, they are distinguished from label-relevant passages by a higher knowledge level. The framework treats them as positive examples, and its retrieval objectives aim to favor and retrieve them more effectively.

l: label-relevant passages, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Label-relevant passages are a biased subset of question-relevant and knowledge-relevant passages, typically sharing high token overlap with the answer label. Retrievers trained solely with negative log-likelihood favor them because they support answer labels, even when not question-relevant. This preference can miss other knowledge-relevant passages and overfit training data, motivating proposed mitigating objectives.

l: KILT, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: KILT organizes generative QA on MSMARCO and informative conversation on Wizard of Wikipedia, supplying that dataset, official scripts, and metrics including R-Precision, Recall@5, KILT-RL, and KILT-F1.

l: Informative Conversations, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: is_a KIG task It is one of the two KIG tasks evaluated in the experiments. It is studied using the Wizard of Wikipedia dataset organized by KILT.

l: retrieval quality, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Retrieval quality is the focus of a proposed framework that seeks diverse, knowledge-relevant passages. It is positioned against KG-FiD, KGI, RE2G, Hindsight, and RAG, and reports 12.1% Recall@1 improvement on MSMARCO and 8.9% R-Prec improvement on KILT-WoW as evidence of more robust retrieval.

l: BART, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: BART is a sequence-to-sequence encoder-decoder model that takes a question, passage, and prior output tokens to generate response-token probabilities, but suffers hallucination in knowledge-intensive generation tasks.

l: retrieval marginalization, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: Retrieval marginalization trains a retriever toward a final task goal by marginalizing retrieval, mitigating false-negative passages; it has improved retrieval quality only limitedly for generative question answering.

l: false-negative passage problem, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: is_a passage labels not being fully annotated [in retrieval-based tasks] The false-negative passage problem refers to passage labels that are not fully annotated in retrieval-based tasks. Ni et al. (2021) found that it occurs frequently in multi-document question tasks, appearing in more than half of the sampled answerable questions in the IIRC dataset.

l: DPR, Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
s: DPR is a Dense Passage Retriever retrieval model that computes inner-product similarity between a question and every corpus passage, selects top-n passages, and uses normalized scores for retrieval and generation. Its passage encoder is fixed for comparison, while initialization uses Natural Questions; as a non-finetuned baseline, it reports MSMARCO and KILT-WoW results.
